# Not all AI is the same [5 min]{.time} {#tool-types}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can name the two tool types they will use this weekend, say what each is for, and run the flow's first question: does the task carry patient identifiers?

**Have ready.** The slides only. No tool open, nothing live in this topic.

**Clock.** 0:00 two types, what each reads and gives (2:00). 2:00 the flow (1:15). 3:15 four tasks in the chat (1:45).

**Watch for.** The flow read as a ranking of brands: it sorts jobs. "So I use Vera Health for everything": a literature tool is not for writing your letters. Product names beyond the ones on the slides: name only ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, Vera Health and OpenEvidence, Sahl AI and Augnito.

**If asked.** A general assistant can search now, so is it a literature tool? Some can search and show links; treat links as leads to open. A literature-grounded tool is built around published papers. Is a literature tool always right? No: it can misread a source, and a cited paper may not say what the sentence claims, so open it. Which assistant is best? The course makes no ranking claim; test on your own task. Can I paste patient details into a literature tool? For a consumer tool, no. For one your institution has approved, that is your institution's decision: ask the data protection officer or legal team.

**Bridge.** "A tool can be excellent and still be closed to you. That is the next topic."
:::

## Two types, two jobs {#tool-types-table}

::: {.lane .sm}
[General assistant]{.node .dark .grow} [Reads: its training, and what you paste in]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [Gives: wording and structure. No built-in citations]{.node .out .grow}
:::

::: {.lane .sm}
[Literature-grounded tool]{.node .dark .grow} [Reads: published papers]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [Gives: an answer with the papers shown. Access varies by country]{.node .out .grow}
:::

[▲ Assistant: drafting, structuring, reasoning through a case. Literature tool: anything where a citation matters.]{.pointer}

[Examples: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini · Vera Health, OpenEvidence. Two more types come on Day Two: ambient scribes, and features built into your institution's record system.]{.muted .small}

::: notes
**2:00.** Asking a general assistant for a citation, and asking a literature tool to write your referral letter, are the same mistake: right question, wrong tool. Top lane: a general assistant is for wording and structure. By default it answers from training, with no source you can open. Some can search and show links; treat links as leads to open, not as proof. Second lane: a literature-grounded tool answers from published papers and shows them. It is not for writing your letters, and access varies by country, which is the next topic. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are examples of the first type; Vera Health and OpenEvidence of the second. Ambient scribes and record-embedded features are Day Two.

**Do.** Stay on the slide. No tool open. Point to each lane as you read it.
:::

## Pick the tool by the job {#tool-flow}

::: {.lane .sm}
[1 · Patient identifiers in the task?]{.node .grow} [yes →]{.op} [STOP]{.node .red .grow} [no ↓]{.op}
:::

::: {.lane .sm}
[2 · A simple fact lookup?]{.node .grow} [yes →]{.op} [Search engine, or your usual reference]{.node .out .grow} [no ↓]{.op}
:::

::: {.lane .sm}
[3 · A citation you can open?]{.node .grow} [yes →]{.op} [Literature-grounded tool]{.node .out .grow} [no →]{.op} [General assistant]{.node .out .grow}
:::

[▲ Ask in this order. A no on line 1 or 2 sends you down a line.]{.pointer}

> **No patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop.**

::: notes
**1:15.** Safety first: the first question is about the patient, not the tool. Walk down the lines. Does the task involve patient identifiers? If yes, stop, and read the privacy line aloud, word for word. If no, go down a line. Is it a simple fact lookup? Then a search engine, or your usual reference. If not: do you need a citation you can open? Then a literature-grounded tool; if not, a general assistant. The flow sorts jobs, not brands. And a tool you signed up for yourself is not an approved tool, whatever its type.

**Do.** Point to each line as you read it. Say "stop" clearly on line one.
:::

[Chat · 1 min]{.tag} Type your four answers in one message, in task order.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Answers:** 1 G. 2 L, then open the citation. 3 S. 4 STOP.
:::

**1:45.** Four tasks, one answer each: where does it land? Type your four answers in one message, in task order, using the letters on the slide. Give people sixty seconds; typing is slower than thinking. Then read out three or four answers and click for the answers. One: general assistant. Two: a literature-grounded tool, and then open the citation. Three: a search engine. Four: stop. Make sure the group hears "stop" on task four, even if it draws a laugh.

**Do.** Run the chat move. If the chat is quiet, ask two people to unmute and give their answer for task two.

# Same tool, different doctor [5 min]{.time} {#different-doctor}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can say why access is part of a tool, and knows the three checks to run before recommending one.

**Have ready.** Nothing live: do not sign up for anything on the call. Say "as of September 2026" aloud each time you give a fact about either tool.

**Clock.** 0:00 the same job, with the vote (0:45). 0:45 who can get in (1:30). 2:15 "GDPR compliant" is not approval (1:30). 3:45 the three checks (1:15).

**Watch for.** "OpenEvidence is bad": it is not; as of September 2026 it is closed to this audience. "Vera Health is better": the claim is only that it does the same job and, on its published terms, does not exclude this group; nothing in the course depends on it. "GDPR compliant" heard as "safe for patient data". Dropping the date.

**If asked.** I can get into OpenEvidence another way; should I use it? Access rules belong to the tool and change; I will not suggest ways around a verification requirement. Check its own sign-up page and your institution's policy. Is Vera Health approved by my hospital? I cannot know; "GDPR compliant" does not answer it. Is GDPR compliance enough for Saudi patients' data? It is a statement about European law; ask your institution's data protection officer or legal team. What happens to what I type? Read the tool's own statement; I will not state a product's policy from memory.

**Bridge.** "Now let us see two tools side by side, on one question."
:::

Vera Health does the same job: citation-grounded answers from peer-reviewed literature. Two tools, one type, one job. The lesson is access, not these two names. Nothing in this course depends on either.

:::

## Access is part of the tool [As of September 2026]{.pill} {#geography}

::: {.lane}
[OpenEvidence]{.node .dark .fixed} [→]{.op} [Requires US NPI verification, and withdrew from the EU and UK in April 2026, so it is not usable by a Saudi audience.]{.node .ghost .grow}
:::

::: {.lane}
[Vera Health]{.node .dark .fixed} [→]{.op} [States that it verifies healthcare professionals globally, with no geographic restriction. Its Terms add conditions.]{.node .out .grow}
:::

[▲ Same job, different doctor. Dashed: not available to you.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**1:30.** As of September 2026: say the date aloud. OpenEvidence requires US NPI verification and withdrew from the EU and UK in April 2026, so it is not usable by a Saudi audience. Vera Health states that it verifies healthcare professionals globally. Its Terms require users to be healthcare professionals in practice or in training, and bar people in countries under US trade sanctions or embargoes; Saudi Arabia is not among those named. How credentials are checked is not published, so try it a few days early, as a bonus. The lesson is access, not these two names. Nothing in this course depends on either.

**Do.** Point to the dashed box: this one is closed to this audience. Say the date again for the second line.
:::

## "GDPR compliant" is not "approved here" {#gdpr-not-approval}

[As of September 2026]{.pill}

::: {.lane}
[Vera Health states that it is GDPR compliant]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [A statement about European data-protection law]{.node .grow}
:::

::: {.lane}
[Approved by your institution?]{.node .ghost .grow} [Suits Saudi requirements?]{.node .ghost .grow}
:::

[▲ The statement does not tell you either of these two.]{.pointer}

[Ask your institution's data protection officer or legal team.]{.big}

[This course is education, not legal advice.]{.muted .small}

::: notes
**1:30.** Vera Health states that it is GDPR compliant. That is a statement about European data-protection law. It does not tell you whether your institution has approved the tool, or whether it suits Saudi requirements. Ask your institution's data protection officer or legal team. This course is education, not legal advice; Day Three covers what the Saudi law says about health data. And a tool you signed up for yourself is not an approved tool, whatever it says about compliance.

**Do.** Point to the two dashed boxes: the statement does not answer them. Read the third line aloud, slowly. Say once that this is education, not legal advice.
:::

# Live demo: same question, two tools [5 min]{.time} {#live-demo}

::: notes
**Goal.** The group has watched one question go to two tools, has voted the grid together, and knows what one run can and cannot tell them.

**Have ready.** Before the call, not in the five minutes: two windows side by side on fresh chats, your general assistant and your second option, whichever you can open (a literature-grounded tool, your assistant's search or citation mode, or a literature search such as PubMed; a clinician colleague's account or a volunteer's shared screen also works). Share your whole screen. The question in a note: general, from your own field, one you can judge, not the Lab One default. Rehearse once; keep screenshots of both full answers, no account name showing, as a fallback.

**Clock.** This is your demo: you run it on the shared screen, the group watches and may paste the same question into their own assistant. 0:00 the second option (0:40). 0:40 the question to both tools (0:50). 1:30 the grid, row by row (2:40). 4:10 what one run can tell you (0:50).

**Watch for.** A horse race: refuse a winner, kindly. The nicer formatting winning applause. A citation that will not open: that is data, say so. Patient detail added "to be realistic": do not.

**If asked.** Which one won? One question, one run, one day; what matters is what each let you check. The assistant gave a citation; is it real? Open it; a made-up citation looks exactly like a real one. The second option cited papers, so is it correct? A citation is something to open, not proof.

**Bridge.** "Now the last habit before the break: how to spend what your plan gives you."
:::

## What one run can tell you {#one-run}

::: {.lane}
[One run of one question]{.node .dark .grow}
:::

::: {.fan}
[▼]{.a} [▼]{.a}
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .teal}
[You can conclude]{.t}

- What each showed: a source, a limit, or nothing.
- How much checking each needs.
- Which to open first.
:::
::: {.card .dashed}
[You cannot conclude]{.t}

- That one tool is better.
- That a citation means the answer is right.
- That it holds in your specialty.
:::
:::

**A citation you have not opened is a claim you have not checked.**

::: notes
**0:50.** What you can conclude from one run: what each tool showed you, a source, a limit, or nothing; how much checking each answer needs before you would use it; and which tool you would reach for first for this kind of question. What you cannot conclude: that one tool is better or more accurate, because one question, one run, one day is not a benchmark, and the same tool can answer the same question differently next time; that a citation means the answer is right; or that the result holds for your own specialty. A citation you have not opened is a claim you have not checked. In Lab One part 3 you run your own comparison.

**Do.** Name no winner. If a citation is still on screen, click it once and read its first line aloud.
:::

# Spend your quota on purpose [5 min]{.time} {#quota}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can name five habits for spending a limited plan on purpose, and knows what Lab One needs when the break ends.

**Have ready.** The restart time, ready to type into the chat. A ten-minute timer.

**Clock.** 0:00 habit 1, batching (1:15). 1:15 habits 2 and 3 (1:15). 2:30 habits 4 and 5, with the free-tier vote (1:15). 3:45 three tabs for Lab One, then the break (1:15).

**Watch for.** The slide turning into a pricing debate: the course quotes no tiers and no limits, because they change. "Paid" heard as "required": nothing here requires a paid plan. Break overrun: hold the start time, because the lab runs on a clock. Real work in the break: a reminder is enough, no patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool.

**If asked.** Which paid tier should I buy? The course recommends none; find out what your free tier gives you first. What counts as synthesis? Combining many facts into one structured piece, like a discharge summary from a whole admission. Is a chatbot ever better than a search engine for a lookup? For a fact with one right answer, you want the page. Where do I keep my prompts? A note on your phone or laptop, one entry per prompt: title, prompt, and what you check.

**Bridge.** "Ten minutes. Then Lab One: you see it for yourselves."
:::

It differs by tool and changes often, so these are habits, not numbers; the boxes are drawn for this course, not measured. Habit one: batch related questions into one detailed prompt instead of five small ones. The SOAP prompt from Module 2 is a batch: the facts, the format and the constraints in one request, not one request per heading.

**Do.** Point to the top row, then the bottom row. Say once that the picture is illustrative, not a measure of any plan.

## Habits 2 and 3: strong tier, or a search {#quota-jobs}

::: {.lane}
[2 · Synthesis: many facts into one structured piece]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [Your strongest option, paid or premium]{.node .out .grow}
:::

::: {.lane}
[3 · A simple fact lookup: a drug's spelling]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [A search engine: it gives you the page]{.node .out .grow}
:::

[▲ A quick lookup does not need your strongest option. A chatbot writes a sentence about the page.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**1:15.** Two: save paid or premium tiers for synthesis, which means combining many facts into one structured piece, such as a discharge summary from a whole admission. A quick lookup does not need your strongest option. Three: a search engine points you to the page; a chatbot writes a sentence about it. For a fact with one right answer, such as a drug's spelling, you want the page. Nothing here says you need a paid plan.

**Do.** Point to each lane in turn. Stay on the slide.
:::

[Chat · 30 sec]{.tag} Do you know what your free tier lets you do today? Type 1 for yes, 2 for no.
:::

**1:15.** Two more. Four: know what your free tier gives you. Limits differ by tool and change often. Before Lab One, find out how much you can do before it stops, and whether the stronger model or web search is included. Find out before you need it, not in the middle of a clinic. Five: keep your best prompts in a personal library. A prompt that worked once is worth more than a new one written from scratch. Start from the skeleton and the four prompts from Module 2, and add each one that works with a line on when to use it.

**Do.** Run the chat vote and read the count. Anyone who typed 2 has a break task.
:::
